source_text: Quod licet in primo libro uberius actum sit [n169] , tamen et hic vel breviter, quid sentias, exprimamus. Times operi diaboli aliquam deputare substantiam, verum non times Deo non aliquod, sed magnum crimen impingere. Maiorem apud te habet reverentiam natura carnis humanae quam iustitia Dei; quasi enim magnum aliquid, ita substantiam hominis diabolo deputare metuisti et quasi rei non magnae id est iustitiae et sanctitati Dei informationem sceleris appulisti, quasi non tolerabilius fuerit inter duas opiniones, sed utrasque falsas, diaboli operibus deputare carnem quam Dei operibus iniquitatem.
pass_a_gloss: Although this has been treated more richly in the first book, nevertheless here also even briefly let us express what you sense. You fear to depute any substance to the work of the devil, but you do not fear to impinge on God not some, but a great crime. Greater reverence with you has the nature of human flesh than the justice of God; as if something great, so you have feared to depute the substance of a human to the devil, and as if of a thing not great, that is to the justice and holiness of God, you have applied the formation of crime, as if it had not been more tolerable between two opinions, but both false, to depute flesh to the works of the devil than iniquity to the works of God.

lemmas.lexica: LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Although we dealt with this more fully in the first book (see this work 1.52, 64), let us briefly state your meaning here too. You fear assigning any substance to the devil’s work, yet you do not fear fastening a great crime—not merely some small fault—on God. Human flesh’s nature commands more reverence from you than God’s justice. You feared attributing human substance to the devil as though that were an important matter, but attached the formation of wickedness to God’s justice and holiness as though they were unimportant. As if, between two opinions that are both false, attributing flesh to the devil’s works would not be more tolerable than attributing iniquity to God’s works!

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
